plot_extraction.response_text:
A professional Rochester baseball team reluctantly travels to Guelph, Canada, for a lucrative exhibition game during a scheduled day off. Expecting an easy victory over local amateurs, the players are surprised by the Canadians’ exceptional speed, powerful throwing, and brilliant fielding. Rochester remains scoreless while Guelph takes a 2–0 lead.

Desperate to secure his share of the gate receipts, manager Merritt secretly introduces the “rabbit,” an illegal rubber-centered baseball whose unpredictable, increasingly violent bounces make it nearly impossible to field. Rochester exploits it to score fourteen runs. However, the alert umpire insists that Guelph also be allowed to bat with the same ball.

The scheme backfires spectacularly. The powerful Canadians hammer the rabbit all over the field, injuring and humiliating the professionals as they erase Rochester’s lead. Merritt replaces the injured pitcher and tries unsuccessfully to substitute a normal ball, but the umpire catches him. Guelph ties the game, then wins after a line drive strikes Merritt and sends him writhing to the ground. Delighted by his poetic punishment, the Rochester players celebrate while Merritt angrily throws the rabbit into a swamp.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story uses a lively first-person retrospective voice, narrated by a professional ballplayer who speaks as both participant and insider. His viewpoint is collective as often as individual: “I” repeatedly gives way to “we,” making the Rochester team’s shared irritation, pride, fear, and delight the emotional center of the narrative. The narrator is knowledgeable about baseball but not solemn about it. He explains specialist terms and tactics naturally, while treating the players’ vanity, gamesmanship, and physical suffering with amused familiarity.

The tone is comic, boisterous, and increasingly farcical, with a strong undercurrent of poetic justice. The professionals initially regard the Canadian players as provincial “rubes,” but their complacency is unsettled by the locals’ extraordinary speed, strength, and fielding. The illicit “rabbit” ball then turns the game into slapstick chaos and ultimately punishes the men who introduced it. Exaggeration is central to the humor: balls behave like animals, fielders are battered or sent staggering, crowds resemble buffalo or cannibals, and Merritt figuratively shrinks as his scheme rebounds upon him. Physical danger is presented as both genuine and comic, giving the game an “element of tragedy” without disturbing the story’s exuberant mood.

The diction combines standard narrative prose with early twentieth-century American baseball vernacular. The narration includes such period expressions as “twirler,” “grasscutter,” “safe hitting,” “in-shoots,” “stiffs,” “cinch the game,” “up in the air,” and “take your medicine.” Dialogue is heavily colloquial, using contractions, dropped consonants, phonetic spellings, and slang—“fellars,” “goin’,” “hev,” “enny,” and “Gimmee”—to distinguish the rough, informal culture of players, managers, and umpires. Merritt’s speech is especially brusque and money-minded, while the players’ exchanges are full of taunts, complaints, and clubhouse mockery. The locals receive less individualized dialogue and are characterized primarily through their physical prowess and rustic appearance, reflecting the professional players’ initially condescending perspective.

Sentence structure varies with narrative function. Expository passages use long, balanced sentences that explain baseball conditions, the properties of the trick ball, or the players’ reasoning. Action scenes shift toward shorter clauses, emphatic fragments, abrupt exclamations, and sound effects such as “Crack!” and “Bing!” Lists are frequently used for comic accumulation, as when every player invents an ailment to avoid the exhibition game or when the “rabbit” successively humiliates the fielders. Parenthetical qualifications and ironic asides allow the narrator to comment wryly on events without halting the action. Repetition—particularly escalating formulations such as “from indifference we passed to determination, and from that to sheer passionate purpose”—heightens momentum.

The pacing follows a clear comic escalation. A leisurely opening establishes the team’s resentment at losing its day off; the journey and arrival build curiosity; the early innings create frustration as the supposedly inferior Canadians repeatedly make spectacular plays. The introduction of the “rabbit” provides the central reversal. At first it seems to guarantee an easy professional victory, but the inability to remove it from play transfers its destructive force to the Rochester team. From that point, the narration accelerates into a succession of hits, rebounds, injuries, errors, and jeers. The climax comes when Merritt, architect of the scheme, is struck by the ball, after which the brief ending delivers both defeat and moral satisfaction.

Characterization is broad, economical, and caricatural. Players are identified by nicknames, ailments, physical traits, positions, or signature abilities: Deerfoot is the swift base runner, Gillinger the huge captain, Hathaway the aging finesse pitcher, and Merritt the irritable, avaricious manager. Rather than deep psychological portraits, the story offers a vivid ensemble whose members reveal themselves through baseball behavior. Their ethics are flexible—they willingly cheat—but their internal code values toughness, skill, loyalty, and the comic punishment of pretension. Merritt is not condemned abstractly; he is made to “take his medicine” physically and publicly.

Imagery is muscular, kinetic, and often drawn from animals, weapons, machinery, and frontier life. The pitcher’s ball resembles a pea from an air gun; hard hits crack like pistols; the rubber ball behaves like a squirrel or “jumping jackrabbit”; players are compared to cats, tigers, railsplitters, and charging buffalo. Verbs such as “slammed,” “scooted,” “caromed,” “lambast,” “pounced,” and “writhed” keep bodies and objects in vigorous motion. Similes are plentiful, concrete, and hyperbolic, making the action easy to visualize while amplifying its comic violence.

The story’s structure depends on irony and reversal. The professionals resent the exhibition, underestimate their opponents, and resort to deception when honest play fails. Their cheating produces a huge lead, but the same device then becomes uncontrollable and exposes them to the punishment they intended for others. The resulting defeat feels like victory to the narrator because team solidarity and revenge on Merritt matter more than the score or gate receipts. The closing emphasis on the game as the “most memorable” achievement of the “rabbit” preserves the tall-tale quality: the episode is framed less as a moral confession than as a legendary piece of baseball folklore.

Overall, the style is that of a period sports yarn: insider narration, colorful slang, quick dialogue, broad characterization, escalating physical comedy, and an anecdotal plot governed by comeuppance. Its chief effects come from energetic action, affectionate mockery of professional ballplayers, and the transformation of a technical baseball trick into an almost animate agent of chaos and justice.

generation.response_text:
There are ball games a man remembers because he won them, and ball games he remembers because he lost them, and then there are games which remain bright in his mind because somebody else took the medicine.

The most memorable game I ever played belonged to the third class.

It happened when I was covering second base for Rochester, in a season when we had a club good enough to lick anything in our league and vain enough to believe we could lick almost anything outside it. Gillinger was captain and first baseman, a six-foot-three monument with hands like smoked hams. “Deerfoot” Dugan played center and could run down a telegram. Old Hathaway did most of the twirling when brains counted for more than steam. We had youth, age, speed, safe hitting, in-shoots, out-drops, tobacco, confidence, and an assortment of bad tempers. What we did not have was much affection for our manager, Horace Merritt.

Merritt was the kind of manager who could look at a double play and calculate the wear on the ball. He never saw a crowd; he saw so many paid admissions. If a thunderstorm washed out a game, he did not blame Providence for the rain. He blamed Providence for neglecting to send it before the gates opened.

Toward the middle of July we had a scheduled day off. A day off in professional baseball is not twenty-four hours on a calendar. It is a cool lake, a fishing pole, a clean shirt, a long sleep, and the right not to hear an umpire’s voice. We had laid plans for that day with the care ordinarily given to military campaigns.

Then Merritt walked into the clubhouse after a hot extra-inning game and said:

“Pack your grips, fellars. We’re goin’ to Canada in the mornin’.”

For a moment nobody answered. We had just beaten Syracuse in eleven innings, and the clubhouse resembled a hospital after a boiler explosion. Spike Nolan had one shoe off and was examining a blister. Hathaway’s arm rested in a tub of hot water. Deerfoot lay flat on a bench with a wet towel across his face. Gillinger was chewing tobacco with the slow solemnity of an ox considering murder.

“What part of Canada?” I asked.

“Guelph.”

“What for?”

“Ball game.”

That brought every corpse in the room to life.

“On our day off?” said Nolan.

Merritt nodded.

Gillinger removed his tobacco and looked at it, as if hoping to discover legal advice there.

“My grandmother’s dead,” he said.

“Your grandmother died in Buffalo last month,” said Merritt.

“That was my mother’s mother. This is the other league.”

“I got a lame ankle,” said Deerfoot, leaping up to demonstrate it.

“My shoulder’s gone,” said our catcher, Pete Coogan, rotating the wrong arm.

“I’m comin’ down with malaria,” said I.

“Can’t git malaria here,” Merritt snapped.

“I caught it in advance.”

Within thirty seconds every man had developed some affliction, obligation, or bereavement. We had sprains, chills, weak hearts, sick uncles, church engagements, poisoned thumbs, and one threatened marriage. Hathaway, who was thirty-eight and had been in baseball since the invention of foul lines, merely lifted his gray head and said:

“If I pitch on my day off, my arm’ll fall off.”

“Then pitch till it does,” said Merritt. “They guarantee us a good gate. Each player gets a share.”

That softened a few of the younger fellows, but not many. Money is a fine medicine, yet a day off in July is finer. Merritt, however, had signed papers, accepted an advance, and probably spent our share in his imagination.

“You’re goin’,” he said. “They got a local club up there that thinks it can play ball. Farmers, shopkeepers, lumber handlers—stiffs. We’ll give ’em five innings of regular ball, make it look close, then cinch the game and come home. Easy money.”

“Who’s pitching?” asked Hathaway.

“You are.”

Hathaway removed his arm from the hot water and gazed sadly at it.

“Good-by, old friend,” he said.

We rode north the next morning in a humor black enough to smoke the car windows. Merritt traveled in the forward coach and counted tickets, receipts, and prospective dollars. We stayed together and insulted Canada.

None of us had seen Guelph, but that did not interfere with our opinions. According to Nolan, every Canadian wore snowshoes in July. Coogan expected the bases to be slabs of ice. Deerfoot had heard that Canadian baseball allowed the batter to carry the bat around the sacks in self-defense. Gillinger said nothing for an hour, then observed that any country which required a man to work on a day off was unfit for civilized sport.

At the border a customs officer asked Coogan if he had anything to declare.

“Only my arm,” Coogan said. “Merritt’s exporting it without permission.”

The officer looked at him, looked at Merritt, and waved us through. I have always believed he understood the situation.

Guelph surprised us. Instead of a frozen wilderness, it was green and hot, with broad fields, brick buildings, shade trees, and half the population waiting around the station. Boys climbed posts to see us. Men in suspenders discussed our batting averages. Girls waved handkerchiefs. A brass band attacked a tune and followed us toward the grounds as if we were prisoners being marched to execution.

The ball park stood beyond the town, with a good infield, a rough but honest outfield, and temporary stands packed before we arrived. Wagons ringed the fences. People sat on roofs, rails, boxes, barrels, and each other. There were farmers with red necks, factory men with scarred hands, merchants in straw hats, children sticky with candy, and women who seemed to know as much baseball as anybody present. The crowd made a low, steady sound, like buffalo moving beyond a hill.

“That’s a gate,” Merritt said, and his face opened like a cash drawer.

Our opponents were already warming up.

At first sight they confirmed our worst prejudices. Their uniforms did not match. One man wore trousers belonging to a larger relative; another had stockings of two different colors. Their captain, a tremendous fellow named McCreery, had shoulders broad enough to hang an advertisement on. Their shortstop was a narrow, freckled youth who looked as if he had left a plow in the next field. Their pitcher, Baird, was long, loose, and sunburned, with wrists like rope knots.

“Rubes,” Nolan said.

Then Baird threw one.

The ball crossed the plate like a pea shot from an air gun and struck the catcher’s mitt with a report that made Coogan blink.

“Lively rube,” I said.

The freckled shortstop took grounders. He moved neither gracefully nor according to any method we recognized. He simply vanished from one spot and appeared at another. A ball hit ten feet to his left was in his hand before the batboy had time to duck. He threw across the diamond without setting himself, and McCreery caught the ball chest-high with a smack.

Deerfoot stopped laughing.

Their outfielders practiced throws to the plate. The left fielder, a black-haired woodsman called Angus, sent the ball in on a line from deep territory. It did not arch. It traveled like a bullet seeking a grievance.

“They ain’t polished,” Gillinger admitted, “but they’re built terrible.”

We still expected to win. A professional club does not surrender its conceit during warm-up. We had seen minor-league wonders before—men who could perform miracles with no one on base and drop their own caps in a game. Besides, these Canadians were local heroes facing trained players. We intended to let them enjoy themselves, then close the door.

We batted first. Baird struck out Deerfoot on three pitched balls.

Deerfoot returned to the bench wearing the expression of a man who has misplaced a staircase in the dark.

“Couldn’t you see it?” I asked.

“Sure. I saw three of ’em. Never saw the same one twice.”

I went up next. Baird’s first pitch rose under my hands. The second broke away. On the third I got enough wood for a hard grasscutter between short and third. I was already thinking of second base when the freckled youth shot sideways, scooped the ball behind his ankle, turned in the air, and threw me out by two steps.

“That hayseed’s got springs,” I said.

Gillinger slammed a liner toward right. Their second baseman jumped, stretched until he looked eight feet tall, and speared it with one hand.

Three men up; three men extinguished.

The crowd roared with delight. Merritt frowned, not yet from anxiety but because we were making the amateurs look too good without charging extra.

In Guelph’s half Hathaway walked to the box with the melancholy courage of an old soldier. He had no blazing speed left, but he could make a baseball approach the plate from six directions and arrive by none of them. He fed Baird a slow curve, a fast one inside, and a drop. Baird missed all three.

“Now,” Hathaway said when he returned to the bench, “if the rest of ’em are pitchers, we’re safe.”

They were not.

The next batter, the freckled shortstop, beat out a slow roller that Nolan fielded perfectly. The boy ran like a cat escaping a kettle. McCreery followed with a drive that nearly amputated Hathaway at the knee. Hathaway lifted one foot by instinct, the ball passed beneath it, and Deerfoot held the runners to first and third with a splendid throw.

Angus came up. Hathaway coaxed him into a high fly, but it went deep enough to score the runner. Guelph led one to nothing.

“That’ll keep the crowd interested,” Merritt said.

Gillinger turned upon him.

“If we get ’em any more interested, they’ll eat us.”

During the next three innings we learned that the Canadians could field anything which remained within the limits of the province. Nolan punched a safe-looking hit over second; Angus sprinted in from left, crossed behind short, and caught it at his shoe tops. Coogan drove one against the right-field wind; their fielder ran back without looking, turned at the last instant, and took it over his shoulder. Hathaway laid down a bunt fine enough to roll along the chalk, but Baird pounced on it like a tiger, threw from his knees, and got him.

We hit hard, soft, high, low, fair, and nearly foul. They caught everything. When they could not catch it, they knocked it down. When they could not knock it down, somebody backed them up. From amusement we passed to irritation, from irritation to determination, and from determination to that passionate state in which nine professionals try to murder a ball because a village club has wounded their dignity.

The harder we tried, the more remarkable those Canadians became.

Meanwhile they gathered another run. McCreery doubled off the center-field fence in the fourth. The blow sounded like a pistol shot and left a dent in the boards. A sacrifice moved him over, and a long fly brought him home.

Two to nothing.

The crowd was no longer merely interested. It had become a weather system. Hats flew, bells rang, children shrieked, and an elderly woman behind our bench informed Gillinger that her sister could bat better than he could.

“Bring her down,” Gillinger called. “We need her.”

At the end of the fifth Merritt met us beside the water bucket. He had lost the prosperous glow he wore at the gate. His mouth looked as if it had been fastened with wire.

“What’s the matter with you loafers?” he demanded.

“They’re good,” I said.

“They’re stiffs!”

“They’re two runs better than these stiffs,” said Gillinger.

“You fellars are throwin’ the game.”

That was dangerous language. Gillinger rose slowly. When Gillinger rose slowly, sensible men moved quickly.

Hathaway pushed him back.

“Save it,” the old twirler said. “If we kill him here, we got to carry him home.”

Merritt glanced toward the grandstand, then toward the Guelph bench. He motioned Coogan and me close.

“I got somethin’,” he muttered.

“So has Pete,” I said. “His is a strained shoulder.”

“Shut up. Look.”

From inside his coat Merritt drew a baseball. It appeared ordinary—white leather, red seams, regulation size—but he held it gingerly, as if it might bite.

I knew what it was. Every old ballplayer had heard of the rabbit, though few admitted using one. A rabbit was built with a rubber heart. Where an honest baseball contained tightly wound yarn around a modest center, this outlaw had enough spring in it to furnish a hotel mattress. Off a bat it traveled farther and faster. On hard earth it did not bounce according to geometry, common sense, or Christian teaching. It struck a pebble and changed its mind. It crouched, leaped, kicked, doubled back, or climbed a man. And the more it was hit, the warmer and livelier its rubber center became.

“That ain’t legal,” I said.

Merritt showed his teeth.

“You want your share of the gate?”

“I want my face.”

“Gimmee the game ball when we go in. I’ll make the switch.”

Gillinger had come close enough to hear. His code of ethics was flexible where victories were concerned, but he did not like Merritt’s tone.

“Suppose the ump spots it?”

“He won’t.”

“Suppose Guelph gets to hit it?”

“They won’t. Soon as we’re ahead, foul it over the stand and put the regular ball back.”

It was a mean scheme, a cheap scheme, and a scheme unworthy of trained athletes.

Naturally, after looking at the score, we agreed to it.

The umpire was a square-built local named Wetherby, with pale eyes and a voice that could halt logging machinery. He had handled the game well and given neither side favors. That made the trick more risky. But when we came in for the sixth, Merritt lounged near home plate complaining about a scuff on the ball. Coogan tossed it to him. Merritt rubbed it, turned his back for no more than a second, and pitched the rabbit to Baird.

I was first to bat.

The rabbit came in high. I swung late and chopped it straight down. It struck in front of the plate, bounded ten feet over Baird’s head, landed behind second, shot sideways away from the center fielder, and was still hopping indignantly when I reached third.

The park became silent except for Merritt.

“Run, you fool!” he screamed.

I scored standing up while Angus chased the ball toward left field. He finally trapped it beneath both knees and looked at it with personal suspicion.

The crowd laughed. So did we. At that stage the rabbit was funny because it hated Canadians.

Deerfoot came next and hit a little bounder toward third. The third baseman charged. The ball dipped under his glove, struck his shin, caromed toward short, hit the freckled youth’s foot, and bounded into the visitors’ dugout. Deerfoot reached second.

Nolan slapped one through the box. Baird got both hands on it. The rabbit climbed his wrists, struck him under the chin, and fell behind the mound. Deerfoot scored, tying the game.

Then Gillinger came up.

“Don’t kill it,” I told him.

He swung.

Crack!

The rabbit went between the left and center fielders with a noise like torn canvas. It struck the ground once and sprang against the fence eight feet high. Angus caught it on the rebound, but it kicked from his hands and rolled under a wagon outside the grounds. By the time a boy retrieved it, Gillinger had lumbered around all four bases, puffing like a locomotive pulling a courthouse.

After that there was no baseball. There was a riot conducted with scorekeeping.

Coogan hit a grasscutter that rose over the second baseman’s shoulder. Hathaway bounced one off third base; it flew into the grandstand. Baird threw carefully, recklessly, inside, outside, and finally nowhere near the plate, but the rabbit would not permit order. If we missed it, we walked. If we touched it, it performed.

The Guelph fielders were superb, brave, quick, and doomed. They flung themselves upon the rabbit and came away empty-handed or bruised. McCreery blocked a hard bounder with his chest; it dropped at his feet, then bounced between his legs. The shortstop made a wonderful stop deep in the hole, but his throw struck the ground before first and vaulted thirty feet over the baseman’s head. Their right fielder caught a fly cleanly, only to have the ball spring from his glove as though insulted by confinement.

Around and around we went. We batted through the order twice and started a third journey. We scored fourteen runs.

The crowd’s laughter turned to astonishment, then anger. They knew baseball. They had seen bad innings, strange hops, and clubs go up in the air. Nobody had seen the earth itself join the visiting team.

Merritt was wild with happiness.

“Foul it out!” he kept calling. “Lose it! Knock it over!”

We tried. That was the first warning that the rabbit had begun managing the game.

Nolan aimed foul and hit fair. Coogan tried to lift it over the roof and popped to the catcher. I deliberately sliced a pitch toward the right-field stand, but the rabbit curved back and landed inside the line. Finally Gillinger swung at a ball near his eyes and sent a towering foul beyond third.

The rabbit rose above the grandstand. Every Rochester player breathed out.

Then a boy on the roof caught it in his cap.

“Throw it here!” shouted Wetherby.

Merritt ran toward the stand waving both arms.

“Keep it, son! Souvenir!”

The umpire fixed him with those pale eyes.

“Throw—that—ball—here.”

The boy obeyed. Wetherby examined the rabbit, weighed it, squeezed it, and looked at Merritt. Merritt smiled with the innocence of a burglar found under a bed.

“Lively ball,” the umpire said.

“Hot weather,” Merritt replied.

“Same ball stays in play.”

“We always change after a big inning.”

“You’ll change after the game.”

Merritt’s smile disappeared.

“But—”

“Your club hit it,” said Wetherby. “Their club hits it. Take the field.”

We went out leading fourteen to two, and never have twelve runs felt so small.

Hathaway stood on the mound holding the rabbit at arm’s length.

“I won’t pitch this thing,” he said.

“You got to,” Merritt called.

“It’s swelled.”

It had. The seams appeared tight, and the ball seemed warm even from where I stood. Every blow awakened the rubber center further. It was no longer a ball. It was a jumping jackrabbit with fever.

Baird, the pitcher, led off for Guelph. Hathaway tried a slow curve. The rabbit refused to curve. It went straight over the plate, and Baird met it.

Bing!

The ball passed Hathaway’s ear, struck the center-field ground, bounded over Deerfoot’s head, and smacked the fence. Deerfoot wheeled. On the second bounce it cleared him coming back. Baird made third.

“Keep it down!” Merritt yelled.

Hathaway looked toward our bench.

“Come out here and sit on it!”

The freckled shortstop hit the next pitch at Nolan. Spike set himself beautifully. The ball struck six feet in front of him, shot to his right, then appeared to reconsider and knocked his cap off on the left. One run scored.

McCreery came up.

I had watched that giant hit an honest baseball against the fence. I now considered the rabbit in his hands and moved backward until I could smell the outfield grass.

Hathaway delivered an in-shoot. McCreery stepped and lambasted it.

Crack!

The ball came toward me three feet off the ground. There are moments when a man’s training conquers his intelligence. I could have ducked. I should have ducked. Instead I put up my glove.

The rabbit struck the heel of it, folded my wrist against my chest, and carried glove, hand, and myself backward. I performed half a somersault and landed with both legs pointing toward Canada.

When I sat up, the ball was rolling in right field. McCreery was on second, and Gillinger stood over me.

“How many fingers?” he asked.

“On who?”

“You’re all right.”

Angus hit one at Gillinger. It struck first base, bounded into his stomach, and dropped him like a felled tree. Another run scored. The next batter drove a liner off Hathaway’s thigh. The old twirler spun twice, sat down, and remained there.

Merritt ran out.

“You hurt?”

“No,” Hathaway said. “I always pitch sittin’ down.”

“Can you keep goin’?”

“My leg’s numb.”

“Then it can’t hurt.”

Hathaway stared up at him. “Horace, if I could stand, I’d kill you.”

The crowd cheered this sentiment.

Merritt had to replace him. Our relief pitcher, Lefty Grove—not the famous Lefty, but a smaller, more nervous article—came in without warming up. Merritt met him near the foul line and tried to slip him another ball.

Wetherby saw it.

“Hold on!”

Merritt jerked his hand behind him.

“What?”

“Gimmee that.”

“This is our warm-up ball.”

“Gimmee it.”

Merritt surrendered an honest baseball. Wetherby put it in his pocket, then pointed to the rabbit lying near second.

“That one.”

“You can’t make us use a dangerous ball!”

“You introduced it.”

“I never!”

The umpire stepped close enough to inspect Merritt’s tonsils.

“Take your medicine.”

That phrase traveled through the crowd. Ten thousand Canadians repeated it with pleasure.

“Take yer medicine, Merritt!”

“Give him a spoon!”

“Open wide, Horace!”

Merritt shrank visibly. At the beginning of the day he had seemed tall enough to count gate receipts over everybody’s shoulder. Now he looked no larger than a batboy caught stealing apples.

Lefty took the rabbit and pitched.

The Canadians fell upon him like woodsmen attacking a pine. They did not try to place their hits. They swung from the roots. Every contact was a pistol crack. Balls scooted between us, over us, under us, and occasionally through us. Deerfoot chased one to the fence, had it bounce back past him, caught it barehanded on the next rebound, and threw toward the plate. The rabbit hit a clod halfway in, turned north, and rolled to the Guelph bench.

Three runs scored.

Coogan attempted to block a low pitch with his chest protector. It climbed beneath his mask and rang it like a dinner bell. He tore off the mask, threw it down, and announced he had retired from baseball. Wetherby told him to put it on.

Nolan stopped a grounder with his knee and began hopping in a circle. Gillinger took a throw at first; the rabbit sprang from his mitt and struck an innocent coach. I dived for a liner, missed it by a yard, and congratulated myself on still possessing teeth.

Run after run crossed the plate.

Our fourteen-run carnival had been comic because it happened to strangers. The Canadians’ reply contained what Hathaway afterward called an element of tragedy. We were battered, scraped, stretched, trampled, and jeered. Yet beneath our suffering ran a disgraceful current of delight, because every bruise landed upon Merritt’s scheme.

At fourteen to eleven he ordered us to bear down.

“At what?” Gillinger shouted. “The ball ain’t there long enough!”

At fourteen to twelve Merritt threatened fines.

“Fine the rabbit!” said Coogan.

At fourteen to thirteen Lefty walked two men rather than pitch across the plate. Wetherby called him over.

“If you keep throwin’ away, I’ll order you to pitch underhand.”

Lefty looked at Merritt. Merritt looked at the gate, as if hoping his money might rescue him.

McCreery came up with two out and the tying run on third. Lefty floated one shoulder-high. The giant chopped it. For once the rabbit behaved like a decent baseball. It rolled straight toward Merritt, who had stationed himself just outside our bench, too nervous to sit.

“Foul!” Merritt cried before it reached the line.

It was fair by two feet.

The ball struck a stone.

Bing!

It leaped sideways and hit Merritt just above the ankle. He gave a howl, seized his leg, and danced into fair territory while the runner scored. McCreery reached first. The game was tied.

No Rochester player hurried to assist our manager. Gillinger leaned on his knees, helpless with laughter. Hathaway, reclining beside the bench with his leg bandaged, beat the ground with his cap. Even Lefty smiled on the mound, though he was facing a powerful Canadian with the winning run aboard.

Merritt limped behind the bench and ordered us to finish them.

Angus stepped in.

Lefty’s first pitch nearly struck him. The second bounced over Coogan’s head. McCreery reached second. With first base open, common strategy called for a walk, but strategy had packed its grip and left Guelph several innings earlier.

“Pitch to him!” Merritt screamed. “They’re amateurs!”

Angus’s face showed no opinion. He merely tightened his blackened hands on the bat.

Lefty threw.

Crack!

The line drive went past the mound at about the height of a man’s belt. I moved one step toward it and then stopped, because Merritt, limping back along the edge of the field to continue his advice, had wandered directly into its path.

The rabbit struck him squarely below the ribs.

There was a sound between a drumbeat and a grunt. Merritt folded around the ball. For one astonishing instant he seemed to sit upon nothing. Then he rolled over, clutched his middle, and began writhing in the dust.

The rabbit caromed into foul territory.

McCreery crossed the plate with the winning run.

The stands erupted. Men threw hats; women waved parasols; boys came over the fence like a tribe of young cannibals. Angus was carried toward the clubhouse. Baird disappeared beneath a heap of teammates. The band played three tunes at once. Somewhere a bell rang without stopping.

We lost fifteen to fourteen.

We were professionals, and pride required us to appear dejected. We tried. Gillinger covered his mouth with his glove. Coogan bent double as if in grief. Nolan buried his face against my shoulder. But when Merritt rose at last, pale and furious, with dust in his hair and both arms wrapped around his stomach, our discipline broke.

We cheered him.

Not loudly at first. A few handclaps. Then Hathaway called, “Take your medicine, Horace!” and the whole Rochester club let go.

Merritt cursed us individually and collectively. He fined Gillinger, released Hathaway, suspended Coogan, and threatened to leave the rest of us in Canada. Since he could scarcely walk and had to ride to the station beside the team physician, none of these punishments possessed much authority.

Wetherby found the rabbit near the foul line and handed it to him.

“Your property,” the umpire said.

Merritt snatched it.

On the road from the grounds we passed a green swamp edged with reeds. The crowd still followed us at a festive distance. Merritt halted, drew back his arm, and hurled the rabbit far out over the brown water.

It struck with a splash.

Then it bounced.

I swear it bounced twice upon the surface—once like a skipped stone, once like a live thing making for shore. Merritt stared at it in horror. Gillinger removed his cap. Hathaway, leaning on two of us, offered a solemn farewell.

The rabbit vanished among the reeds, carrying with it fourteen runs, a manager’s dignity, and what remained of our day off.

We collected our shares of the gate a week later. Merritt deducted for damaged uniforms, lost equipment, medical treatment, and what he called insubordination. My portion scarcely paid for the wrapping on my wrist. Hathaway was not released, Coogan was not suspended, and Gillinger’s fine disappeared after the captain explained that Merritt might otherwise have to find a new first baseman, second baseman, catcher, center fielder, and pitching staff.

Years afterward, whenever Rochester players gathered, somebody would mention Guelph. We never spoke first of the Canadians’ speed, though it was marvelous; nor of Baird’s pitching, though he had shut us out with an honest ball; nor of McCreery’s hitting, which could have frightened artillery. We spoke of Nolan’s cap, Gillinger’s stomach, Coogan’s ringing mask, my backward somersault, and Hathaway sitting on the mound.

Last of all, we remembered Merritt folding around that line drive while the winning run came home.

We lost the game, our pride, and most of the gate money. Yet when I reckon up the victories of my career, I count Guelph among the sweetest.

For a man may forget a pennant, but he never forgets the afternoon a rabbit made his manager take his medicine.

## The Cartographer of Lost Roads

On the morning the road disappeared, Mara Vale was painting a mountain that did not exist.

She sat at her drafting table in the eastern room of the Royal Map House, where the windows were tall enough to catch sunrise before it touched the palace towers. Beneath her hand lay a sheet of calfskin, smooth and pale. Upon it, in shades of gray and blue, rose the Frostback Range: seven peaks, three glaciers, a narrow pass marked with a red dotted line.

Mara had never seen the Frostbacks. No living person had.

They had vanished eighty-two years earlier.

“Your shadows are wrong,” said Master Orin.

He had entered without a sound, as he always did. He leaned over her shoulder, smelling faintly of dust, lavender soap, and the bitter tea he drank throughout the day.

“The light comes from the west,” Mara replied.

“The light comes from where the king says it comes from.”

Mara glanced at the official compass rose pinned above her desk. By royal decree, all maps showed illumination from the east, because the king’s capital lay in the east and therefore, according to court scholars, was the source of all civilization, wisdom, and metaphorical light.

She turned back to the mountains. “Then the king’s light makes poor shadows.”

Master Orin’s mouth almost became a smile.

“Careful,” he said. “You’re talented enough to be overheard.”

He placed a folded message beside her inkstone. The paper bore the green seal of the Department of Roads.

“Another correction?” she asked.

“Not a correction.”

She opened the message.

At dawn today, the southern highway between Bellweather and Saint Orra ceased to exist. Surveyors dispatched. Traffic suspended. Map House assistance requested.

Mara read it twice.

“Ceased to exist?”

“So they claim.”

“Roads don’t simply disappear.”

Master Orin looked at the Frostbacks on her table. “No. Of course not.”

By noon, Mara was riding south with a military escort.

The highway began just beyond the capital’s wheat fields. It was broad, white, and straight, built in the reign of King Tomas II, who had loved roads because they allowed taxes to travel efficiently in one direction and soldiers in the other.

For three hours, nothing seemed unusual. Carts passed carrying wool and barley. Pilgrims walked toward Saint Orra, their staffs wound with green ribbons. Mile stones stood at regular intervals, each carved with the royal lion.

Then the highway ended.

Not at a gate, a landslide, or a broken bridge. It simply stopped.

The white stones gave way to a meadow of waist-high grass shimmering under the wind. No ruts continued through it. No crushed weeds marked the passage of yesterday’s carts. Wildflowers bloomed where the road should have been, as if they had grown undisturbed for decades.

A crowd had gathered at the edge. Merchants argued with soldiers. A woman knelt in the grass, searching for something. A priest sang a protective hymn in a wavering voice.

Captain Pell, leader of Mara’s escort, dismounted.

“How far does it go?” he asked the nearest surveyor.

“We don’t know.”

“How can you not know?”

The surveyor pointed.

A hundred paces into the meadow, the land dipped into a shallow valley. Beyond it stood a forest.

Mara unfolded the official road map. There was no forest. According to the inked lines, the highway should have continued across open farmland, passing three villages before reaching Bellweather.

“Where are the farms?” she asked.

The surveyor swallowed. “Gone.”

“And the villages?”

“Gone.”

“People?”

“Gone as well.”

The kneeling woman cried out. She had found a small wooden horse beneath the grass. One of its wheels was missing.

“My son’s,” she said. “He dropped it from our cart yesterday.”

Captain Pell helped her stand. “Where were you traveling?”

“Home. To Bellweather.”

“Your son is there?”

“My husband, too.”

She clutched the toy to her chest and stared across the meadow.

Mara walked to the final paving stone. Its edge was clean, not broken. She placed one boot on the grass.

The world tilted.

For an instant she smelled rain on hot stone and heard hundreds of distant bells. Images flashed before her: towers drowning in sand, ships sailing through fields, a silver door beneath an elm tree. Then the meadow returned.

“Mistress Vale?” Captain Pell said.

She realized he had caught her arm.

“I’m fine.”

“You went pale.”

Mara looked down. At her feet, half-hidden among the roots, was a milestone covered in moss. She crouched and scraped it clean.

The carved number read 47.

The last visible milestone on the highway, ten paces behind them, read 19.

“This place is old,” she said.

The surveyor frowned. “The grass?”

“The distance.”

That evening, they established camp where the road ended.

Mara worked by lantern light, comparing records. In the Royal Atlas, the highway to Bellweather crossed twenty-eight miles of farmland. In an older map from the Map House archives, copied before the highway was built, the same region was covered by forest. An even older map showed a valley containing a lake called Orison Mere.

The lake had disappeared three centuries ago, drained by royal engineers.

Yet when night fell, frogs began calling from somewhere beyond the hill.

Mara woke after midnight to find Master Orin sitting beside the dead fire.

She did not scream, though she nearly did.

“You weren’t with us,” she whispered.

“I took a shorter road.”

“There is no shorter road.”

“There used to be.”

In the moonlight he looked older than he had that morning. His face sagged around his sharp bones.

Mara glanced toward the sleeping soldiers. “You knew this would happen.”

“I feared it.”

“What is happening?”

Master Orin rubbed his hands together for warmth. “What is a map?”

“A representation of a place.”

“That is what we teach apprentices.”

“It’s the truth.”

“No. It’s the first lie.”

He took Mara’s map and spread it across his knees.

“A map is a decision,” he said. “It decides what matters. This river has a name; that stream does not. This border is real; that path is forgotten. This city belongs here. That village never existed.”

“Symbols don’t change the land.”

“Don’t they?”

He touched the painted Frostback Range on the map.

“Long ago, cartographers merely recorded the world. But over centuries, as maps were copied, studied, trusted, and obeyed, something changed. The world began listening.”

Mara thought of mountains no living person had seen, yet whose shapes every apprentice memorized.

“The Frostbacks,” she said.

“Were erased from the atlas during a border dispute. A generation later, explorers found a plain where the mountains had stood.”

“That’s impossible.”

“Yes.”

The frogs continued their unseen chorus.

Master Orin pointed toward the meadow. “When King Tomas built the southern highway, his mapmakers removed the old forest, straightened streams, renamed villages, and drew the road before its stones were laid. Reality followed. Slowly at first. Then completely.”

“If maps command the world, why has the highway vanished?”

“Because something older has begun to speak.”

He drew a black book from beneath his coat.

Its cover was cracked, its corners furred with age. There was no title, only a circle stamped around a four-pointed star.

Mara recognized it from forbidden references in the archive index.

“The First Atlas,” she breathed.

“Not the first. But the oldest surviving.”

He opened it carefully.

The pages were crowded with roads. Some ran between cities. Others ended at sketches of trees, wells, standing stones, or tiny houses. Along the margins, scribes had written notes in many hands.

A good path for winter.

Avoid the woman in the blue field.

This bridge appears only to liars.

Here I dreamed of my dead brother and woke with his ring.

“These aren’t official surveys,” Mara said.

“They are memories. Journeys. Stories. For most of history, maps were made by those who traveled, not those who ruled. A road existed because people walked it and remembered where it led. But the crown gathered every map under one authority. One vision replaced thousands.”

“And now?”

“Now the forgotten roads want to return.”

Master Orin turned to a page marked by green thread. It showed the region south of the capital—not as fields, but as layers of forest, lake, marsh, farms, paths, and ruins, all drawn over one another.

“The world can bear many memories,” he said. “But not forever. The king’s maps have held it rigid for generations. Something has cracked.”

“Can we restore the highway?”

“Yes. If we redraw it strongly enough.”

“Then why haven’t you?”

“Because restoring one road will erase everything beneath it again.”

Mara looked toward the darkness where frogs called from a lake that had not existed for three hundred years.

“The villages on the highway,” she said. “The people living there.”

“They may return if the road does.”

“May?”

“Maps are decisions. Not promises.”

At dawn, they entered the meadow.

Captain Pell objected until Master Orin showed him a document bearing the king’s private seal. Then the captain objected more quietly.

The woman whose family had vanished insisted on joining them. Her name was Elian, and she carried her son’s wooden horse in a pouch at her belt.

The four of them crossed the grassy valley.

At its lowest point, Mara’s boots sank into mud. Water gleamed between reeds. Ahead, the forest waited beneath a blue morning haze.

They reached the first trees before noon. The trunks were immense, their roots humped like sleeping animals. No highway passed among them, but a narrow trail appeared whenever Mara looked away and vanished when she stared directly at it.

Master Orin followed without hesitation.

“What road is this?” Mara asked.

“One I took as a child.”

“Here?”

“Not exactly.”

The trail wound deeper into the forest. Birds called in unfamiliar voices. Once, Mara glimpsed a stone wall running between the trees. Another time, they crossed a bridge over a dry riverbed, and Captain Pell’s armor dripped water for an hour afterward.

Near sunset, they found a house.

It stood in a clearing, white-walled and roofed in red tile. Smoke rose from its chimney. Beside the door grew an apple tree heavy with golden fruit.

Elian ran forward.

“Wait,” Master Orin called.

The door opened. A boy of six stepped out.

“Mother?”

Elian fell to her knees. The boy rushed into her arms.

A man followed, weeping and laughing. Elian held them both, touching their faces as if afraid they might dissolve.

Mara felt joy rise in her, then stop.

Behind the house lay other cottages, their windows glowing. A narrow village street curved into the trees.

“This isn’t Bellweather,” she said.

Elian’s husband looked at her. “Bellweather?”

“Your home.”

He shook his head. “This is Orison.”

Orison Mere, Mara thought.

The lake drained three hundred years ago.

Master Orin whispered, “We must leave.”

Elian stood, holding her son. “I’m staying.”

“You don’t understand,” Mara said. “This village doesn’t belong to your time.”

“My family is here.”

“They may not be what they seem.”

The boy reached into Elian’s pouch and took out the wooden horse.

“My horse,” he said.

He turned it over. Its missing wheel was intact.

Elian looked at Mara with tears on her face. “They’re exactly what they seem.”

The village bells began to ring.

Not alarm bells. Evening bells. Doors opened along the street, and people emerged carrying lamps. Some wore modern coats and factory boots; others wore tunics, furs, or robes from centuries past. A soldier in rusted armor walked beside a girl holding a paper parasol. An old woman carried a clay jar painted in a style Mara had seen only in museums.

All of them were people whose roads had been erased.

Captain Pell crossed himself.

The villagers watched without hostility, but their silence felt like a warning.

Master Orin pulled Mara back toward the trail. “Now.”

“What happens to them if we redraw the highway?”

His eyes answered before he did.

“They vanish.”

Elian took her husband’s hand. “Then don’t redraw it.”

“The capital needs the southern road,” Captain Pell said. “Grain, medicines, troops—”

“The capital has other roads.”

“Not enough.”

“There are always other roads,” Master Orin said. “That is the lesson kings refuse to learn.”

They left Elian beneath the apple tree.

Her son waved until the forest closed around them.

On the return journey, the paths shifted. Captain Pell followed a trail marked with white stones and vanished between one step and the next. They searched for hours, shouting his name. At last they found his sword standing upright in the mud beside a battlefield where pale soldiers fought noiselessly beneath a red sky.

Master Orin would not let Mara enter.

“He chose a soldier’s road,” he said. “We cannot follow.”

“You speak as if the road chose him.”

“Is there a difference?”

They continued alone.

By the time Mara saw the meadow again, three days had passed, though the military camp looked abandoned for years. Tents sagged beneath moss. Vines wrapped the wagons. On the final paving stone, someone had carved a message:

THE KING COMMANDS THE ROAD RESTORED.

Beneath it rested a case of mapmaker’s tools.

Mara opened the case. Brushes, compasses, inks, gold leaf, measuring cords—everything needed to draw an official road into being.

Master Orin sat heavily in the grass.

“You said it could be restored,” Mara said.

“It can.”

“How?”

“Draw it from here to Saint Orra. Name every bridge and milestone. Mark the villages as they were on the latest royal survey. If your map is accepted into the Royal Atlas, the highway will return.”

“And Orison?”

“Gone.”

“Elian?”

“Gone.”

“Captain Pell?”

“Perhaps returned. Perhaps not.”

Mara lifted a bottle of black ink. It looked ordinary.

“How many times have you done this?”

Master Orin was silent.

“How many?”

“Enough.”

The word carried a great weariness.

“You erased places.”

“I preserved kingdoms.”

“You erased people.”

“I saved more than I erased.”

“Did you count them?”

“At first.”

Mara wanted to hate him, but his hands were trembling.

The light faded. In the west, the sky burned gold behind clouds shaped like distant mountains.

“What happens if I refuse?” she asked.

“The old roads continue returning. Not only here. Everywhere. Rivers will remember former courses. Cities will overlap with ruins. Borders will unravel. The world may become impossible to navigate.”

“Or it may become larger.”

“Those are often the same thing.”

They spent the night beside the broken highway.

Mara dreamed she stood in the Royal Map House surrounded by blank pages. Outside, the capital’s towers drifted like ships. A thousand roads led from her desk, and along every one walked a different version of herself.

In the morning, Master Orin was dead.

He sat against the milestone with his coat buttoned neatly, the First Atlas in his lap. His face was peaceful.

On the final page, he had written a note.

Forgive us for teaching you that only one world could be true.

Mara buried him beneath the meadow.

Then she began to draw.

For seven days, she worked.

She drew the southern highway from the capital to Saint Orra, but not as the king had commanded. She drew the white road and the forest path beneath it. She drew Orison Mere under the wheat fields, and the drowned chapel whose bell still rang in winter. She drew Bellweather, the vanished farms, the ancient village, and the battlefield under the red sky.

Where two roads crossed, she did not choose between them.

She painted both.

In the margins she wrote what she remembered.

Here Elian found her son.

Here Captain Pell followed the stones.

Here Master Orin took a shorter road.

Here the frogs sing after midnight.

When she finished, the map was too crowded for royal use. Roads twisted across one another. Villages occupied the same hills. Rivers branched into past and present courses. It was not clear, efficient, or obedient.

It was beautiful.

Mara carried it north.

The return journey took less than a day. The capital appeared at sunset, but its walls had changed. One tower was covered in ivy; another shone with new copper. Gates from different centuries stood side by side, each opening onto a different street.

No guards stopped her.

The Royal Map House was in chaos. Apprentices ran through halls carrying atlases. Officials shouted conflicting orders. Maps peeled themselves from the walls. Painted ships moved across parchment seas, searching for ports erased long ago.

In the eastern room, Mara found the Royal Atlas open on its iron stand.

The king was there.

He was younger than she expected, dressed in a plain black coat, with ink stains on his fingers. Ministers and guards surrounded him.

“You are Vale?” he asked.

“Yes, Majesty.”

“You were ordered to restore the road.”

“I have mapped it.”

She placed her work before him.

His expression hardened as he studied it.

“This is unusable.”

“Only if you wish to use one road at a time.”

“There must be one correct map.”

“There has never been one correct map.”

The ministers murmured. The captain of the guard drew his sword halfway.

The king raised a hand.

“If I put this in the Atlas,” he said, “what will happen?”

“I don’t know.”

“You are the cartographer.”

“I am a cartographer. That is different.”

Outside, bells rang in towers that had not existed that morning.

The king walked to the window. Below, the capital unfolded in overlapping streets. Citizens wandered between old gardens, new marketplaces, ruined walls, and canals remembered by the earth. Some were frightened. Others stared in wonder.

“My advisors say the city will collapse,” he said.

“It might.”

“They say trade will fail.”

“It might.”

“They say enemies will cross forgotten roads and appear inside our walls.”

“They might.”

He turned. “You offer little comfort.”

“Comfort is not the same as truth.”

“And what truth does your map offer?”

Mara looked down at the layered roads.

“That no place belongs only to those who rule it now. That every road leaves something behind. That erasing what is inconvenient does not destroy it. It only teaches it to return in secret.”

The king remained silent for a long time.

Then he dismissed the guards and ministers.

When they were alone, he touched a small path Mara had drawn through the forest.

“My sister vanished on a northern road when I was ten,” he said. “The official account says she drowned.”

“What do you remember?”

“A door beneath an elm tree.”

Mara recalled the vision she had seen when she first stepped into the meadow.

She opened the First Atlas. Near the northern border, faint lines gathered around the drawing of a silver door.

“This road may still exist,” she said.

“Can you find it?”

“Perhaps.”

The king closed his eyes.

Then, with both hands, he lifted the old Royal Atlas from its stand.

It was enormous. Its jeweled cover bore the weight of four centuries of decrees. He carried it to the fireplace and dropped it into the flames.

The pages caught slowly.

Borders blackened. Roads curled. Seas turned to smoke.

All across the city, stone groaned.

Mara placed her map on the empty stand.

For one breath, nothing happened.

Then the windows flew open.

Wind rushed through the Map House, scattering papers into the sky. Blank sheets spun above the capital like white birds. On the streets below, doors appeared in walls, bridges arched over forgotten rivers, and lanes unfolded toward places no decree had named.

Far to the south, a white highway ran through fields toward Bellweather.

Beside it, visible between ancient trees, a narrow path led to a village beneath an apple tree.

Both were real.

Neither was safe.

Years later, travelers would speak of Mara Vale, the first Royal Cartographer to refuse the title. She became instead the Keeper of Roads, though she insisted the roads kept themselves.

Under her guidance, maps changed.

They were no longer printed as final authorities. Every inn kept a local chart to which guests added warnings, memories, and discoveries. Children learned that north could shift, that a bridge might remember another river, and that a road appearing on no official page could still lead home.

Some people hated the new world. Merchants cursed paths that changed with the seasons. Soldiers complained that borders had become uncertain. Tax collectors found entire towns relocating into earlier centuries to avoid them.

But lost families also returned.

Forgotten languages were heard in market squares. Extinct flowers bloomed beside factories. The Frostback Mountains reappeared one winter at the edge of the western plain, their seven peaks casting long, perfectly incorrect shadows toward the east.

As for the king’s sister, Mara found the silver door in the tenth year of her travels.

It stood beneath an elm tree on a hill that existed only during thunderstorms. The king, older and no longer dressed in black, accompanied her.

Beyond the door lay a sunlit garden.

A woman waited there, no longer a child and not yet old. She held a book in one hand and a cup of tea in the other.

“You took your time,” she told her brother.

While they embraced, Mara sat beneath the elm and unfolded a fresh sheet of paper.

She drew the hill first, then the storm, then the silver door.

At the bottom she left a wide blank space.

Every map, she had learned, needed room for a road that had not yet decided where to go.
